description: Core Concept: Identifying terrestrial locations on Earth—such as deserts, polar regions, and caves—that share topographical and environmental characteristics with the Lunar and Martian surfaces. ​Objective: Providing analog environments for space mission teams to test equipment, validate technologies, and train before actual spaceflight.
summary:
**ENGLISH (about 200 words)**

TerraLunaMars is a screening model that studies candidate Moon and Mars sites by comparing them with well-documented analogue sites on Earth, using open NASA, ESA and USGS data.

The problem: choosing where to land or build on the Moon or Mars requires knowing slope, surface texture, rock type and thermal extremes. Field study is impossible before a mission, and orbital data is hard to interpret without a familiar reference.

Our solution: we compare each target with a geologically similar site on Earth, so terrain can be examined on the ground, not only from orbit. We built two pairs: Flaugergues Crater on Mars with the Lut Desert in Iran, and the Gruithuisen Domes on the Moon with Sugarloaf Dome in Arizona.

Method: we used MOLA, LOLA and Copernicus DEM GLO-30 data, resampled each pair to one grid and window, and computed relief, slope, roughness and elevation scatter in Python.

Results: Mars and Lut reached 86.3% topographic similarity, and Moon and Sugarloaf 74.1%. Lut is best framed as a hyper-arid wind-erosion analogue, not a thermal one.

Limitations: 68.4% of the Mars window is interpolated, and gravity, atmosphere and temperature differ. This is a screening tool, not proof of equivalence.

Code, report and results: github.com/nil258199-coder/TerraLunaMars
details: What does the project do? TerraLunaMars is a screening model for Moon and Mars sites. It compares each target with a geologically similar site on Earth, using open terrain data, so planners can understand slope, roughness, relief and rock context from a familiar reference. We built two pairs: Flaugergues Crater (Mars) with the Lut Desert (Iran), and the Gruithuisen Domes (Moon) with Sugarloaf Dome (Arizona). How does it work? We select comparable sites, assemble open NASA MOLA, LRO LOLA and ESA Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data, and resample each pair to one grid and analysis window. Python then computes relief, slope, local roughness (after removing the regional trend) and elevation scatter. Similarity per metric is S = 100 x (1 - |a - b| / max(|a|, |b|)). We also scored 19 indicators across geology, topography, temperature and mineralogy, and combined them into an equal-weight index. What are its benefits? It gives a consistent first screening step before mission resources are committed. Anyone can recompute, audit and challenge the metrics. It also bridges terrestrial field geology with planetary data, and it shows clearly which aspects match (topography, wind erosion) and which do not (temperature). What is the intended impact? To help narrow where to look and which hypotheses to test for future Moon and Mars landing or base sites, such as the Gruithuisen Domes, the planned Lunar-VISE target in 2027. It does not replace mission data. Its impact is making questions about other worlds measurable and open to verification. Tools, languages, devices and software used Python (NumPy, including numpy.gradient for slope) for the terrain metrics, Google Colab for running the analysis, and GIS for the initial comparison. Data: NASA PDS (MOLA MEGDR, LRO LOLA), ESA Copernicus DEM GLO-30, USGS Astrogeology, NASA Earth Observatory. Gemini NotebookLM helped organise sources and slides, Claude supported coding and drafting, and Manus accelerated the interface and code build. GitHub hosts the report, atlas and results. How is the project creative, and what factors did the team consider? The idea links three bodies (Terra, Luna, Mars) through Earth analogues, turning hard-to-read orbital numbers into something familiar. We considered scientific honesty throughout: a strict same-grid rule so results measure the ground, not the grid; clear labels separating computed values from literature estimates; open reporting of limits (68.4% of the Mars window is interpolated, window size affects results, gravity, atmosphere and temperature differ); and bilingual English-Arabic material so the work is accessible. We also chose the analogue’s process, not the planet, as the basis for comparison.
